moduleTitle: The nature of God: omnipotence, beneficence, mercy, fairness and justice/Adalat in Shi'a Islam, immanence and transcendence

note.specFocus: Know the nature of God: omnipotence, beneficence, mercy, fairness and justice (Adalat in Shi'a Islam), including different ideas about God's relationship with the world: immanence and transcendence.
note.summary:
Muslims believe God cannot be fully described, but He has revealed something of His nature through His names. Tradition speaks of the 99 'Beautiful Names' (al-Asma' al-Husna), e.g. al-Khaliq (Creator), al-Alim (All-Knowing), al-Ghaffar (Forgiving). Muslims often recite them with prayer beads (subhah/misbaha).

OMNIPOTENCE
God is all-powerful (al-Qadir): 'Allah is over all things competent' (2:20). He creates by command: 'His command when He intends a thing is only that He says to it "Be", and it is' (36:82). Implications: trust in God (tawakkul), belief in al-Qadr, and accepting that God can do what humans cannot understand. Raises questions about suffering and free will.

BENEFICENCE
God is ar-Rahman, the Most Gracious / Beneficent - generous and loving to all creation. He provides the world, food, rain, family, guidance and life itself. Surah 55 (ar-Rahman) repeatedly asks 'Which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?'. Muslims respond with gratitude (shukr) and by caring for creation as khalifah (stewards).

MERCY
God is ar-Rahim, the Most Merciful. 113 of the 114 surahs begin 'Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim'. 'My mercy encompasses all things' (7:156). Hadith qudsi: 'My mercy prevails over My wrath'. God forgives those who sincerely repent (tawbah) - 'do not despair of the mercy of Allah' (39:53). Muslims are to show mercy to others.

FAIRNESS AND JUSTICE / ADALAT
God is al-Adl, the Just. 'Allah does not do injustice, even as much as an atom's weight' (4:40). He judges everyone fairly on the Day of Judgement, taking account of intentions and circumstances. For Shi'a Muslims Adalat is one of the five roots of Usul ad-Din: God is perfectly just by nature, so He does not compel people to sin and then punish them - humans therefore have free will. It also motivates Muslims to act justly (5:8) and resist oppression, as Imam Husayn did at Karbala.

IMMANENCE AND TRANSCENDENCE
- Transcendent: God is beyond the universe, time and human understanding: 'There is nothing like unto Him' (42:11); 'Vision perceives Him not' (6:103). Hence no images of God (aniconism) and great reverence.
- Immanent: God is close and active in the world: 'We are closer to him than his jugular vein' (50:16); 'I am near; I respond to the call of the caller' (2:186). Hence personal prayer (du'a) and a sense that God sees every action.
Muslims hold both together (57:3, 'the Outward and the Inward'): transcendent in essence, immanent in knowledge, power and care. Sufi traditions emphasise closeness through dhikr; many theologians stress transcendence to avoid making God like humans.

TENSIONS FOR EVALUATION
- Mercy vs justice: resolved by repentance offered fairly to all.
- Omnipotence and benevolence vs suffering: suffering seen as a test (2:155) with justice in the hereafter.

KEY TERMS: al-Asma' al-Husna, ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim, al-Adl, Adalat, tawakkul, tawbah, du'a, dhikr.

questions.question:
Which word means that God is beyond and outside the created universe?
A Immanent
B Transcendent
C Beneficent
D Omnipotent
questions.modelAnswer: B - Transcendent means God is beyond the world and human understanding; immanent is the opposite idea of God being close and active within the world.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one letter is credited; if you change your mind, make your final choice clear.

questions.question:
What does the Shi'a term 'Adalat' refer to?
A God's mercy
B God's justice
C God's power
D God's oneness
questions.modelAnswer: B - Adalat is the Shi'a root of faith stating that God is perfectly just and never acts unfairly.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one letter is credited; if you change your mind, make your final choice clear.

questions.question: Give two of the names or qualities of Allah.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: ar-Rahman (the Most Gracious / Beneficent); ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful); al-Adl (the Just); al-Qadir (the All-Powerful / omnipotent); al-Alim (the All-Knowing); al-Khaliq (the Creator); al-Ghaffar (the Forgiving). Accept English qualities such as merciful, just, omnipotent, beneficent.
questions.examTip: Two brief, accurate points earn the two marks - no development is needed, so don't waste time. Don't give two versions of the same point.

questions.question: Give two ways Muslims believe God shows His beneficence.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: creating the world and everything humans need; giving life and the natural world (food, water, rain); sending prophets and holy books for guidance; giving humans intelligence and free will; providing for every creature; offering forgiveness.
questions.examTip: Two brief, accurate points earn the two marks - no development is needed, so don't waste time. Don't give two versions of the same point.

questions.question: Explain two contrasting Muslim beliefs about God's relationship with the world.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. God is transcendent: He is beyond the universe, outside time and space, and cannot be fully understood or pictured. 'Vision perceives Him not' (6:103). This is why Muslims never make images of God and use names rather than descriptions.

2. God is also immanent: He is close to every person and involved in the world. The Qur'an says 'We are closer to him than his jugular vein' (50:16). Muslims therefore believe God hears every private prayer (du'a) and knows their thoughts, so He can be approached directly at any time.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways/beliefs. For each, make the point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, explanation or consequence (second mark).

questions.question: Explain two ways belief that God is merciful influences Muslims.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It encourages Muslims to repent and not give up. Because God is ar-Rahim, Muslims believe that sincere repentance (tawbah) brings forgiveness, so a person who has done wrong is motivated to change rather than despair, e.g. by asking forgiveness in prayer during Ramadan.

2. It encourages them to be merciful to others. Nearly every surah starts 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful', and Muslims are taught to imitate God's mercy by forgiving people and helping those in need, for example through zakah, sadaqah or volunteering at food banks.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways/beliefs. For each, make the point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, explanation or consequence (second mark).

questions.question:
Explain two Muslim beliefs about the nature of God.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. God is omnipotent (all-powerful). The Qur'an repeats that 'Allah is over all things competent' (Qur'an 2:20). Muslims believe God created the universe simply by commanding 'Be' (kun) and it was, so nothing is beyond His power, and believers can trust Him in every situation.

2. God is merciful. Each surah except one begins 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful', and in a hadith qudsi God says 'My mercy prevails over My wrath' (Bukhari and Muslim). This means Muslims see God not only as a judge but as loving and forgiving, which gives them hope.
evidence: Hadith qudsi: 'My mercy prevails over My wrath'

questions.question:
Explain two reasons why belief in God's justice (Adalat) is important to Shi'a Muslims.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It guarantees that judgement will be fair. 'Indeed, Allah does not do injustice, even as much as an atom's weight' (Qur'an 4:40). Shi'as believe this means God would never punish people for actions they were forced into, so humans must have genuine free will and are responsible for their choices.

2. It inspires Muslims to work for justice in the world. Since God is just, His followers must be too: 'O you who believe, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice' (Qur'an 5:8). For many Shi'as, Imam Husayn's stand against the unjust ruler Yazid at Karbala is the supreme example, encouraging them to stand up against oppression today.

questions.question:
‘God cannot be both merciful and just.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING THE STATEMENT
Some people argue there is a tension between mercy and justice. Justice means giving people exactly what they deserve - punishing wrongdoing and rewarding good. Mercy means letting people off what they deserve. If God forgives a murderer who repents, it may seem unfair to the victim; if He always punishes, He would not be merciful. Critics, including some atheists, also ask how a just and merciful God could allow so much suffering of innocent people, for example in natural disasters, and conclude that He cannot have both qualities perfectly.

The Qur'an describes both Jannah and Jahannam, and some people find it hard to see eternal punishment as merciful, or forgiveness of serious crimes as just.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE STATEMENT
Muslims believe God is both, and the Qur'an presents them together. God is al-Adl (the Just): 'Allah does not do injustice, even as much as an atom's weight' (4:40). God is also ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, and 'My mercy encompasses all things' (7:156). Muslims argue that God's mercy works within His justice: He offers forgiveness to those who sincerely repent, which is fair because everyone is offered the same chance. A hadith qudsi says 'My mercy prevails over My wrath', which suggests mercy is the greater quality but does not cancel justice.

Shi'a Muslims stress Adalat as a root of faith, and argue that because God is just He gives humans free will and never punishes anyone for something they could not avoid. Mercy is shown in His giving guidance through prophets and Imams, so people are not judged without being warned. Also, only God knows everything about a person's circumstances, so He can judge with perfect justice while taking into account what humans cannot see, such as intentions (niyyah). Suffering in this life may be a test (2:155), with reward in the hereafter, which balances out what seems unfair now.

CONCLUSION
The objection works if justice and mercy are understood in purely human, legal terms. However, Islam teaches that God's knowledge is complete and that He sets fair conditions for mercy - repentance and faith - which apply to everyone. Since a perfectly wise judge could combine strict fairness with generous forgiveness, I conclude that the statement is not convincing: God can be both merciful and just, although the problem of suffering remains a serious challenge for believers to think through.
questions.examTip: Use the four bullet points as a plan: Muslim teaching, arguments for, arguments against, justified conclusion. Higher levels need logical chains of reasoning and a judgement that weighs the arguments - not just a list. Spelling, punctuation and grammar may also be credited on 12-mark answers.

questions.question:
‘It is impossible for God to be both immanent and transcendent.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING THE STATEMENT
At first these two ideas seem to contradict each other. Transcendence means God is beyond the universe, outside time and space and completely unlike anything created: 'There is nothing like unto Him' (42:11) and 'Vision perceives Him not' (6:103). Immanence means God is present within the world and close to people. Some argue that if God is wholly 'other' and beyond creation, He cannot also be inside it in a personal way, and if He is close and involved, He is no longer completely beyond.

A non-religious thinker might add that both claims are untestable, so describing God as both just shows that the concept is incoherent.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE STATEMENT
Muslims believe the Qur'an teaches both, so they must be compatible. 'We are closer to him than his jugular vein' (50:16) expresses immanence, and 'He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward' (57:3) shows both together. Many scholars explain that God is transcendent in His essence - what He is - but immanent in His knowledge, power and care. Being outside creation does not stop Him knowing and sustaining every part of it, just as an author is not a character in a book but knows every word of it.

Muslims experience both: God's transcendence explains why they do not picture Him and why He is worthy of total worship; His immanence explains why they can make personal du'a at any time and believe He answers: 'I am near; I respond to the call of the caller when he calls on Me' (2:186). Sufi Muslims especially emphasise closeness to God through dhikr (remembrance), while still affirming His transcendence. If God is all-powerful, it would be strange to say He is unable to be close to His creation.

CONCLUSION
The two ideas would contradict each other if they described God in the same way at the same time. But Islam teaches that God is beyond the world in His being and close to it in His knowledge and care. This gives a coherent picture of a God who is both worthy of awe and approachable, so I disagree with the statement: it is possible, and important for Muslims, that God is both immanent and transcendent.
